query: Consider the following context: How to rationally design composition of alloys with desired properties has always been an open and challenging question, especially for high-entropy alloy (HEA) which has huge selections of composition due to the feature of multi-principal elements. Although great efforts have been made in the past decades, such as approaches based on thermo-kinetic analysis and simulations, strategies to quick determine the optimal HEA composition remain lacking. In that context, which method can be used for design intrinsically strong, ductile, and low-weight refractory HEA (RHEA) compositions, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Integrating machine learning models with high-throughput experimental data and thermodynamic databases will enable rapid identification of refractory high‐entropy alloy compositions that are simultaneously intrinsically strong, ductile, and low in weight.
generation.material_initial_state: A vast compositional pool of unoptimized refractory high‐entropy alloys that have not yet been tuned for the optimal combination of strength, ductility, and low density.
generation.intervention: Apply a data-driven inverse design strategy using machine learning models trained on high-throughput experimental results, CALPHAD thermodynamic outputs, and historical alloy data to predict promising RHEA compositions.
generation.conditions: The screening and predictions are performed under conditions representative of both ambient and elevated temperature mechanical testing, with computational resources enabling parallel high-throughput evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: The resulting alloy microstructures, such as a body-centered cubic matrix possibly with targeted precipitate phases and controlled local lattice distortions, which mediate enhanced strength, ductility, and reduced density.
generation.mechanism: By learning complex correlations between composition, thermodynamic parameters, and resulting microstructure-property relationships, the machine learning model can efficiently navigate the vast high-entropy compositional space. This approach infers combinations that achieve the desired balance of elemental contributions to lower density while promoting mechanisms (e.g., lattice distortions and precipitation strengthening) that enhance both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: A set of RHEA compositions predicted to achieve improved mechanical performance (higher strength and ductility) with reduced weight compared to alloys designed through conventional thermo-kinetic or brute-force simulation approaches.
generation.baseline: Traditional design approaches involving high-throughput CALPHAD or thermo-kinetic simulations that are computationally expensive and slow to pinpoint the optimum compositions in the vast compositional space.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis may not hold if the available training data and thermodynamic databases lack sufficient accuracy to capture unforeseen microstructural phenomena or if the machine learning model's predictions fail to generalize to unexplored compositional regimes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in mechanical properties and the extent of the weight reduction remain uncertain until validated experimentally; additional complexities such as oxidation behavior and processing variability could affect outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a set of refractory HEA compositions predicted by the integrated machine learning framework and a control set designed using traditional CALPHAD-based screening. Subject both sets to standardized mechanical testing at room and elevated temperatures, and compare measured tensile strength, ductility (elongation), and density. In addition, use microstructural characterization via X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy to confirm the predicted structures.
measurements: Tensile strength (e.g., yield strength, ultimate tensile strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RHEA compositions selected by the machine learning approach do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (both higher strength and ductility with lower density) compared to the traditional approach within a minimal threshold improvement, then the hypothesis that the data-driven method offers a rapid and effective pathway for design is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system. The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. In the example of the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system, it takes only a few hours on a desktop computer to finish the HTCs (~ 3 × 10 3 ) within the composition range of 5–50 at.% for each element and finally screen out eight potential alloys. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
